questions.q: Name the crystalline salt most commonly found in human renal calculi and state the urinary condition that promotes its precipitation.
questions.a: Calcium oxalate is the most common constituent; precipitation occurs when urine becomes supersaturated with calcium and oxalate ions due to low urine volume (concentrated urine) or hypercalciuria/hyperoxaluria. A wrong answer like "uric acid crystals" or "dehydration alone" reveals confusion between stone types and the specific solubility product concept.

questions.q: Explain why hemodialysis fluid (dialysate) is prepared with an electrolyte composition similar to plasma but completely devoid of urea and creatinine.
questions.a: The dialysate mimics plasma osmolarity to prevent net water shift (osmotic balance) and maintain electrolyte gradients for essential ions (Na⁺, K⁺, HCO₃⁻), while the zero concentration of nitrogenous wastes creates a steep diffusion gradient for their removal from blood. A wrong answer focusing only on "removing wastes" misses the critical concept of preventing electrolyte disequilibrium syndrome.

questions.q: A patient with chronic kidney disease (CKD) has a GFR of 12 mL/min, serum potassium 6.2 mmol/L, and hemoglobin 7.8 g/dL. Predict which two complications will NOT be corrected by hemodialysis alone and justify.
questions.a: Anemia (low erythropoietin production) and renal osteodystrophy (impaired calcitriol synthesis) will persist because hemodialysis only replaces filtration/excretion, not the endocrine functions of the kidney. A wrong answer listing hyperkalemia or uremia shows misunderstanding of what dialysis actually clears versus what requires hormonal replacement.

questions.q: Compare the pathogenesis of calcium oxalate stones versus uric acid stones in terms of urinary pH, solubility, and dietary risk factors.
questions.a: Calcium oxalate stones form in neutral to alkaline urine where oxalate solubility is low; risk factors include high oxalate diet (spinach, nuts) and low citrate. Uric acid stones precipitate in persistently acidic urine (pH < 5.5) because undissociated uric acid is poorly soluble; risk factors include high purine intake (organ meats) and gout. A wrong answer that swaps pH dependencies reveals a fundamental confusion about acid-base chemistry of stone formation.

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: "Kidney transplantation from a living related donor is always superior to hemodialysis for a 65-year-old diabetic patient with end-stage renal disease."
questions.a: False. While transplantation offers better long-term survival and quality of life, a 65-year-old diabetic has higher surgical risk, cardiovascular comorbidity, and infection susceptibility from immunosuppression. Hemodialysis may be safer initially. A blanket "always superior" answer ignores individualized risk-benefit analysis required in clinical decision-making.

questions.q: Design a public health awareness poster for a rural Indian community that explains the link between three modifiable lifestyle factors and kidney stone prevention, using only local language concepts (no medical jargon).
questions.a: A good poster would depict: (1) "Drink 8-10 glasses of water daily" (prevents concentrated urine), (2) "Limit salt and pickles" (reduces calcium excretion), (3) "Eat seasonal vegetables, not just spinach/tomatoes daily" (dietary oxalate variety). A poor answer uses terms like "hypercalciuria" or "citrate supplementation" which are inaccessible to the target audience.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Kidney stones (renal calculi)?
questions.a: Students believe hemodialysis "cleans the blood completely" like a filter, not realizing it only removes small solutes by diffusion down concentration gradients — it cannot remove protein-bound toxins, does not replicate tubular reabsorption/secretion, and fails to replace endocrine functions (EPO, vitamin D activation).

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can explain the pathophysiological mechanism of stone formation linking urine concentration and solubility product, describe the principle of hemodialysis using diffusion across a semipermeable membrane, and differentiate between acute and chronic renal failure based on reversibility and treatment options.
